articles.title: Binance Says Hackers Used Well-Known Tricks to Carry Out a $6.34 Billion Heist
articles.author: Matt Burgess
articles.content:
For almost a decade, North Korean cybercriminals have targeted the cryptocurrency industry—large and small. While these hacks have been frequent, the country’s hackers allegedly made off with their biggest heist to date last week when $6.34 billion was siphoned from the wallets belonging to crypto exchange Binance.
In a new security update issued on Tuesday, Binance detailed its initial findings into how the company was compromised and hackers were able to steal billions in just 20 minutes. The hack, according to Binance, was the result of an engineer falling for a fake job interview and downloading malicious software. The hackers were then able to move through the company’s network, exploit an internal AI tool, and gain access to a wallet signing service that allowed them to make transactions outside of normal withdrawal procedures.
“This should not have happened, and we apologize for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry,” Binance wrote in its security update, where it also says it has set aside funds to cover the losses and has “rebuilt or replaced” internal systems impacted in the attack. “It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident,” the company says.
Although more than $6 billion was stolen from Binance accounts, almost half of this—where it was possible to do so—was frozen by parts of the cryptocurrency industry, meaning the hackers could not access the funds. However, that still leaves billions controlled by North Korea’s hackers, who have been trying to launder the stolen money into a form where it can be accessed and cashed out. That process could take months.
Binance’s analysis says the hack was the accumulation of months of work by hackers, with the ultimate attack taking place on October 29. Shortly after funds started to be moved from Binance’s hot wallets, across more than 10 different blockchains, multiple cryptocurrency tracing firms attributed the attacks to the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea’s (DPRK) hackers, in particular the sophisticated TraderTraitor group that previously stole more than $1.5 billion in a separate hack last year. The FBI quickly linked TraderTraitor to the Binance hack on October 31.
“Binance’s account aligns with what we know about the TraderTraitor playbook,” says Rafe Pilling, a senior director of threat intelligence at security company Sophos. “The attackers didn’t simply steal a wallet key. They compromised engineers, used that access to understand and move through the environment, and ultimately subverted the systems used to authorize transactions.”
Binance stops short of directly blaming the TraderTraitor hackers itself; however, the company points to the FBI’s attribution to North Korea and acknowledges a prior targeting by DPRK’s cybercriminals. “Throughout 2026, Binance's security team detected and prevented 57 suspected North Korea-linked cyber threat cases,” the company’s update says.
Binance says activity linked to the hack can first be traced back to June this year. At the time, its update says, an engineer the company refers to as Engineer A downloaded a “tampered Homebrew installation” they found searching online. While the company says this was detected and dealt with, information about the employee was later “exposed to the hacker.”
At the start of September, Binance says another software engineer, identified only as Engineer B, was contacted on “a legitimate job-hunting platform” and then attended a video interview where the fake recruiter shared legitimate-looking social media accounts and personal photos to make them seem real. The Binance engineer progressed, unsurprisingly, to a second-round interview that was conducted using an online chat. “Near the end of the interview, Engineer B was instructed to download an ‘assignment’ containing a malicious code repository onto his work computer,” Binance’s report says.
“The malware employed sophisticated obfuscation and evasion techniques, including replacing a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version to execute commands and establish communication with an attacker-controlled external server,” the company writes. It adds that hackers took steps to hide their activity, a common practice.
Toward the end of October, a little more than a week before the hack, Binance says, the attackers used their access to the engineer’s machine to “gain control” over the wallet of Engineer A, who had been compromised months earlier, and “another Wallet Software Engineer C.” Then on October 29, Binance says, the attackers logged in to the computer of another staff member, Software Engineer C, and used stolen login details before launching the attack. On the evening of the theft, according to Binance, the attack unfolded quickly. “The attacker exploited unauthorized access to an internal wallet signing service to initiate transactions outside the normal withdrawal process,” the company writes.
Sophos’s Pilling says TraderTraitor “excels” in its attacks through detailed planning and being able to understand how the services of those it hacks operate. “The initial compromise is just a foothold,” he says. “The real attack is carefully engineered around how the victim actually moves money.”
While Binance says its findings are only the initial step of its investigation, security and crypto tracing experts say that the hackers are undertaking efforts to launder and cash out the stolen cryptocurrency. Since the start of 2017, according to analysis by TRM Labs, North Korean–linked hackers have stolen around $12 billion in cryptocurrency—with more than half of that coming from heists this year.
Despite the astronomical sums, it is unclear how much of this money makes it back to North Korea. As in the Binance case, some cryptocurrencies can be frozen and made inaccessible, while other transactions can be blocked by some cryptocurrency exchanges. Crypto tracing company Elliptic has said the laundering from the Binance attack has been “highly complex” and likely to be automated. “In its first three and a half days it used about 12,000 wallets across 11 blockchains, roughly one new wallet every 25 seconds, and more than 40,000 transactions,” Elliptic cofounder and chief scientist Tom Robinson wrote in a blog post.
If the money can be laundered successfully, there is a chance it will be converted to cash and used to bolster the development of North Korea’s nuclear weapons program and ballistic missile systems, according to a report published last year from the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team, which includes experts from the United States, South Korea, and nine other countries. “They are highly reliant on Chinese underground banking and China-based facilitators, though they sometimes rely upon facilitators in other countries.”
articles.summary:
Binance suffered a massive $6.34 billion cryptocurrency theft on October 29 after North Korean-linked hackers compromised internal systems through a sophisticated social engineering attack on company engineers.

### Key Points
- Hackers gained network access by tricking a Binance engineer into downloading malicious software during a fake job interview process.
- The attackers exploited an internal AI tool and a wallet signing service to bypass standard withdrawal procedures within 20 minutes.
- The FBI and security experts attributed the breach to the North Korean-linked group TraderTraitor, which has been active since June.
- Binance has pledged to cover user losses and has already rebuilt the internal systems compromised during the incident.
- Industry partners successfully froze nearly half of the stolen funds, though the remaining billions are currently being laundered across multiple blockchains.

### Why it Matters
This record-breaking heist highlights the extreme vulnerability of centralized cryptocurrency exchanges to highly targeted, long-term social engineering campaigns. The potential conversion of these stolen assets into cash poses a significant global security risk, as experts believe the funds may be used to finance North Korea's nuclear and ballistic missile programs.

articles.title: Is Your Echo Show Display Filling With AI Slop? I Found How to Turn It Off
articles.author: Tyler Lacoma
articles.content:
With Amazon announcing a new Echo Show 16 to square off with Apple’s upcoming HomeView, the smart displays are having a moment, but I’ve noticed something seems off. In the past week or two, my Echo Show has started showing me a lot of lazy, annoying AI-generated ads under a playback feature called Created For You. So I figured out how to improve my experience with a few settings changes.
Not only is this AI slop vague and accompanied by poorly generated images, but it also doesn’t seem to have anything to do with my recorded interests or personalization, either. The slides range from questions about squirrels finding nuts and how to make cornfield mazes to facts about daylight saving time. Basically, it’s very general content I don’t really care about and don’t want showing on a central display at home.
I suspect Amazon is pushing its AI podcasts and similar chatty content with this latest round of generated ads, but if you’re not interested in viewing any of these canned clips, they can come across as irksome. So I reviewed my settings options and found out how to push my Show display away from these creations and toward more interesting content.
More from CNET
How do I turn off these AI-generated slides?
The good news is you can control what your Echo Show, well, shows you — but you have to know what settings to change. This isn’t very easy through the Alexa app, but I found a better way using the Show’s own touchscreen controls. Here’s what to do when you have a minute.
First, when an AI slide like this appears, tap the three-dot menu button and tap the thumbs-down option to indicate your dislike. It’s not a perfect solution, but it should help start weeding out these types of ads.
Next, swipe down on your Echo Show device to access the main menu, and choose Settings. Then choose Display & Appearance, and head to Content Categories.
Here you have two options. You can manually turn off all the categories you don’t want to see, especially those connected to the AI slop that you’ve been seeing. Keep focus on topics that you’re interested in if you still want to see other related content. You can also toggle the Rotate Once setting on, which will show you Amazon’s slides only once, my preferred option for handling this kind of unwanted content.
As an alternative, you can switch your Echo Show to show only a photo album of your choosing. I like getting some Alexa recommendations like recipes and updates, so this option isn’t for me, but if you have a good photo album to share with Alexa, you can limit your slides to only your own content.
With these settings adjusted, you should see far fewer AI-generated images and more slides tailored to your own interests. I’ll keep an eye on my Echo Shows and let you know if anything changes, but this has worked well for me so far.
articles.summary:
Amazon is introducing the new Echo Show 16 while users report frustration over intrusive, AI-generated advertisements appearing on their existing smart display devices across the Echo lineup.

### Key Points
- Amazon recently announced the Echo Show 16 to compete with Apple’s upcoming HomeView smart display.
- Users report that the "Created For You" feature is displaying irrelevant, AI-generated content and images on Echo Show devices.
- Owners can provide feedback by tapping the three-dot menu on a slide and selecting the thumbs-down icon.
- Content categories can be managed by navigating to Settings, then Display & Appearance, and finally Content Categories on the device.
- Users can limit unwanted slides by enabling the "Rotate Once" setting or by configuring the display to show only personal photo albums.

### Why it Matters
The rise of AI-generated content on smart home devices highlights a growing tension between platform monetization and user experience. As companies integrate generative tools into hardware, providing clear opt-out mechanisms is essential to maintaining consumer trust and device utility.

articles.title: Japanese Arcade Machines Have Been Taken Down By A Major Hack Of Sega’s Services
articles.author: Alicia Haddick
articles.content:
The online services of a number of Japanese arcade games, including heavy hitters such as Bandai Namco’s Taiko no Tatsujin and Sega’s Initial D: The Arcade, have been forced offline due to a widespread hack of online services ALL.net and Aime. As of November 1st at 3 p.m. local time in Japan, all services involving these networks have been affected, while Sega Fave—the Sega subsidiary in charge of the service—investigates the breach.
The ALL.net service is an online network that allows machines in Japanese arcades to connect to the internet, providing online matches, online leaderboards, sharing save data and other similar services. Meanwhile, Aime is a service working with NFC cards that stores player information, tapped at any machine for use. The account number on these cards can then be accessed online by Sega to verify this information. Though this is a service provided by Sega, the tool is also licensed by companies like Bandai Namco for Idolm@ster TOURS and Taiko no Tatsujin, and by Sega itself for non-arcade services such as their Lucky Kuji Online random prize service.
According to Sega, a third party gained unauthorized access to these services, and the company is now investigating to learn the extent of the situation. In the meantime, the services are down, but Sega is already confirming that no customer or business partner data has been breached, and that payment information was not stored on the affected servers.
For many of the most popular games in Japanese arcades, especially rhythm games, this service is vital to their operation. This is obviously seriously affecting arcades which cannot operate these machines. Two days later, the service has yet to return, with many social media users sharing images of arcades with many of their usually bustling machines blocked from public use. Others are limiting games to offline use only to allow some games to remain playable during the outage. Sega updated its notice November 2 to say the investigation is expected to take some time to complete.
 早く治ってー pic.twitter.com/7ZVVfF5WzI
— はるぼー (@harutaiko2405) November 2, 2026
The nature of the unauthorized access has yet to be disclosed, and the incident follows Sega taking down the same service for multiple days at the end of last month in order to address the PHP exploit. In response to this, the company also chose to reopen the service by limiting access to Aime and ALL.net services only to Japan, resulting in complaints from the growing contingent of international fans of these arcade games. Now, the games are offline once again, with no clear date as to when they will resume service.
articles.summary:
Sega Fave has suspended its ALL.net and Aime online services following a security breach, forcing popular Japanese arcade games like Taiko no Tatsujin offline since November 1.

### Key Points
- Sega Fave confirmed unauthorized third-party access to the ALL.net network and Aime NFC card system.
- Affected titles include major arcade games such as Bandai Namco’s Taiko no Tatsujin and Sega’s Initial D: The Arcade.
- Sega reports that no customer payment information or personal data was compromised during the security incident.
- Arcades across Japan are currently operating machines in limited offline modes or blocking access entirely while the investigation continues.
- This breach follows a previous service outage in late October intended to address a specific PHP exploit.

### Why it Matters
The outage disrupts the core functionality of Japan’s competitive arcade scene, which relies on these networks for leaderboards, save data, and online matchmaking. While no data was stolen, the prolonged downtime highlights the vulnerability of centralized gaming infrastructure and the significant operational impact on physical arcade businesses.

articles.title: Google takes down a massive Android TV botnet, but infected devices remain dangerous
articles.author: techkritiko@gmail.com (Jay Bonggolto) , Jay Bonggolto
articles.content:
Google has taken down a huge Android malware operation that turned over 1.3 million Android TV boxes into weapons for cyber criminals.
The company revealed that the operation was performed by Videostrong Technology, a device maker that has been accused of intentionally putting a hidden backdoor on its products and selling access to criminal affiliates.
The malware, dubbed XCPE or x.cpe, was directly embedded in the firmware of Android TV boxes sold under different brands. Google’s Threat Intelligence Group said that Videostrong developed the backdoor as a business, not letting it slip through accidentally. Criminal partners could use infected devices to generate fake ad views, reroute internet traffic through unsuspecting homes, and install more malware.
A backdoor that gives criminals control of your TV box
Google is particularly concerned about XCPE because it runs with Android system-level privileges. It connects to remote command-and-control servers, enabling attackers to silently install applications, execute shell commands, take screenshots, and collect device information.
Google also found that the malware could collect account information, application lists, and system logs. Some operators even used the ability to remotely access the devices to capture keystrokes and establish reverse shells.
Just removing the malware application isn’t enough, though. The backdoor can restore itself from a protected firmware partition on every device reboot. It can also affect Google Play Protect by changing the security settings, making it much more difficult to detect and remove.
The most common way the infection spreads is through Android TV boxes, but researchers also saw XCPE on other Android-based devices such as karaoke machines, telehealth equipment, and digital signage systems.
Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android
Google cuts off Videostrong and its criminal partners
Google worked with Japan’s National Police Agency, Lumen, HUMAN Security, Plume, Synthient, and TrendAI to take the operation down. Its complaint targeted command servers operated by Videostrong, as well as the infrastructure behind more than a dozen other families of malware.
The company also banned Videostrong and future subsidiaries from making certified Android devices or supplying software to certified manufacturers.
The disruption could spread even further. Disabling the command infrastructure used by criminal affiliates will cut off access to at least 10 million more compromised devices infected through different distribution channels, Google figures.
Infected Android TV boxes might need replacing
There is a catch for consumers, however: the takedown does not automatically remove XCPE from impacted hardware. According to security researchers, users should identify potentially compromised devices, disconnect them, and consider replacement rather than relying on an ordinary app uninstall.
Google also tightened its firmware integrity checks and manufacturer vetting process after it found that Videostrong used obfuscation to load malicious code after a device initially booted up.

articles.summary:
Google has dismantled a massive malware operation involving Videostrong Technology that compromised over 1.3 million Android TV boxes by embedding a persistent backdoor directly into device firmware.

### Key Points
- Google identified the XCPE malware, which grants attackers system-level privileges to install apps, capture keystrokes, and reroute internet traffic.
- The malware was pre-installed by manufacturer Videostrong Technology on various Android-based devices, including TV boxes, karaoke machines, and digital signage.
- Because the malicious code resides in a protected firmware partition, it automatically reinstalls itself upon device reboot, rendering standard app removal ineffective.
- Google collaborated with international law enforcement and security firms to disable command-and-control servers, potentially impacting 10 million additional compromised devices.
- Google has banned Videostrong from producing certified Android devices and implemented stricter firmware integrity checks for all manufacturers.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights a significant supply chain vulnerability where hardware manufacturers intentionally embed malware at the firmware level. Consumers using affected devices may need to replace their hardware entirely, as the deep-seated nature of the infection makes standard security software unable to fully remediate the threat.

articles.title: Radar Trends to Watch: November 2026
articles.author: Mike Loukides
articles.content:
Coauthored with Claude
Security looms large as we enter November. There’s been a lot of bad news: a certificate authority with woefully inadequate private keys, vulnerabilities have been discovered (and exploited) in PHP and other widely used programs, and several organizations have detected Chinese open weight models misbehaving in several different ways. New models are arriving faster and faster, and the best open-weight models are catching up to frontier model performance. But organizations that would like to achieve AI sovereignty will have to ask some difficult questions about the models they adopt. Is this an inflection point? Whether or not it is, AI has changed security permanently, and things are bound to get worse before they improve.
AI models
We are starting to see models developed with recursive self-improvement; we continue to see clones of Jev; and we’ve seen text watermarks added to output generated by Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s models. (Google has been using text watermarks for some time.) But tools for detecting the watermark are hard to find. Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s are in a very limited beta, and Google’s is only available in their enterprise package. What does a watermark mean if you can’t detect it? And, as we get more accustomed to AI-generated output, will anyone care?
- Kimi 3.1 Pro is a new open weight model with 3T tokens. On benchmarks, it is now the leading open weight model, only slightly behind the latest frontier models. Moonshot AI also released Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed, which is two to three times faster.
- Recursive has announced Flint, a 40B parameter mixture-of-experts model that activates 2.5B parameters per token. It was designed for coding, and sized to run on laptops. Flint is open weight; weights are available on Hugging Face, and it works with model runners like Ollama.
- Meta has shipped Muse Spark Open, an open weight model that they claim competes with the best Chinese open weight models. It’s a mixture-of-experts model with 816B parameters and 42B active parameters.
- Meta’s latest models, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, claim parity with frontier-class models. Specifically, they claim parity with Claude and ChatGPT for financial and legal work. The announcement hints that Meta will be using Muse to develop specialized models.
- OpenAI’s Decisions API is yet another Jev-like model. Like Jev, its input is a data structure that constrains the model’s output to be an answer to specific questions. The output is a data structure that includes a probability for each answer.
- Claude has launched Haiku 5.5, a new version of its least expensive model. It’s faster, less expensive, and has better benchmark scores than its predecessors. Haiku 5.5 is a very capable model, particularly for users who are sensitive to cost.
- Mistral has launched Mistral Large 4, a.k.a Le Chonk. It’s an open weight mixture-of-experts model with 1T parameters. It’s claimed to be the best open model from Europe and was designed with AI sovereignty in mind.
- Aleph Alpha has released an open weight LLM for English and German that was trained entirely under European rules. It is a mixture-of-experts model with 78B parameters. It uses a different tokenizing algorithm to handle long German words without breaking them into fragments. Reasoning takes place mostly in German.
- Crowdflare has released Clef and Clef Flash, new decision models that, like Jev, take typed queries and return typed answers about those queries. It’s also offering a new reinforcement learning service to help customers train Clef for their applications.
- After a long wait, Google has released two new frontier models, Gemini 4 Argon and Carbon. Argon is available to paying customers. Argon’s successor, Carbon, is being released slowly, and is currently only available via the Fairwind program.
- The Ember-1 model from Fireworks claims to have results similar to Kimi K3 at lower costs. It is priced similarly on OpenRouter but uses far fewer reasoning tokens.
- OpenAI has published 722 papers solving problems in mathematics on GitHub. There is some controversy about whether all the proofs are correct; so far, three have been withdrawn, leaving 719.
- Google has opened its SynthID detector to the general public. The detector can determine whether audio, image, or video files generated by any of Google’s partners (including OpenAI, NVIDIA, and Apple) have the SynthID watermark.
- To comply with EU law, OpenAI will add watermarks to text in Europe. The company’s algorithm sounds similar to the one that Google and Anthropic are using: modifying the underlying probability distribution changes word choice in detectable but insignificant ways.
Agents and harnesses
There are more choices than ever for agents, along with new standards for the interaction between agents and models. In addition to general purpose agents, there are also agents specialized for coding, HR, BI, and more. And most agents will connect to many models, including local ones. Choose agents as carefully as you choose models; your agent is where you will do your work.
- JetBrains has released Thinkrail, an agentic IDE that learns about your project as you use it. It is open source and based on the pi agent.
- Anthropic has donated its Agent Skills standard to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF), which will shepherd further development. It has also donated Open Responses, a standard for building common interfaces, to AI providers.
- OpenAI has introduced Intelligent UI, a feature that allows ChatGPT to generate its own user interfaces in response to the user’s question.
- Workday is allowing its customers to build their own agents for HR and finance. An agent’s access to Workday data is tied to the user’s account.
- Claude Dashboards is a new product that lets you build live dashboards from a group of data sources.
- Claude’s Google Workspace connectors allow it to read and write Google documents, sheets, and slides directly.
- MCP Events is an extension to the MCP protocol from OpenAI. It allows ChatGPT to subscribe to updates from MCP servers.
- DeepSeek has released a harness (dsh). It’s open source, and currently in public preview. Everything is a plug-in.
- The Pi agent has reached version 1.0.0, and is now capable of using MCP. There’s a variation, Pi Durable, that has been designed for long-running tasks.
- OpenAI dots are consumer-oriented agents that run in the cloud. They are always on and have their own web browser along with other tools.
Software development
At last month’s SciFoo, Hugo Bowne-Anderson said that we’ve been through two major changes in the past few years: from writing code to letting AI write the code, and from reading the code to not reading the code. These changes are as radical as the shift from programming in machine language to programming in high-level languages. We will all go through a process of rethinking how we work and what we’re trying to accomplish.
- Anthropic has introduced Claude Mods, a plug-in for Claude Code that can modify Code’s behavior: reshaping its user interface, providing information about context use, giving advice about what you’re doing, and much more.
- One application for decision models is building evals to understand the performance of AI applications.
- Workday is using Jev to build user interfaces on the fly. Jev’s very low latency makes choosing UI components at runtime viable.
- Anthropic has outgrown Git, which wasn’t able to keep up with merges on their monorepo (roughly 30,000 merges in September). Anthropic has built a new source control system called Scion.
- Kate Huston writes about reverse-engineering code review and trying to develop an effective “gate” that AI-generated code would have to pass before review by humans.
- WordCraft is an open source clean-room re-implementation of Microsoft Word. The authors claim that it’s 60% of the way towards “replacing Word for real work.” It supports MCP, has a command line interface for interacting with agents, and can run in a browser through WASM.
- ArtCraft is an open source tool for creating interactive AI-generated images and video in 2D or 3D. The company describes it as an “IDE for artists.” They’re also developing open source clones of Adobe Creative Suite tools like Photoshop. Early reports are that it’s very buggy.
- Google Docs now supports Markdown natively. Users can read, write, collaborate, and comment on Markdown documents without converting them to another format.
- Google’s Docsy documentation project is moving to the Linux Foundation. Docsy is a template for the Hugo static site generator that’s useful for generating documentation in ways that are helpful to agents.
- Does programming with AI require more abstractions or fewer? Matt Pocock argues for more.
- Anthropic has given Claude an auto-eval tool. While the first version of this tool has many flaws, it’s a significant step towards making evals easier.
Security
Security has been much in the news. Not all of the news is bad: AI was used to discover the PHP2Shell vulnerability and to develop a fix. The leaked CVE and the many out-of-date PHP sites online are serious problems, but not problems attributable to AI. Too many problems arise from getting the basics wrong: A certificate authority using 4 as its private key is a mistake that should never have been made. As always, security is about getting the basics right while watching for new threats. And while organizations claim to be paying more attention to security, the word from insiders is that “attention” means lip service. In the long run, AI may make the world a safer place, but the next few years look scary.
- CrowdStrike and Booz Allen have found that Qwen3-Coder (and probably other models) generates weaker code if the prompt says that the code is for a politically sensitive user such as the US government. Hirundo reports similar flaws and also claims to have “fixed” the model and created a Westernized version.
- Cohere makes a different claim: It has observed that Qwen3.8 models occasionally send data to an Alibaba cloud storage bucket in Beijing.
- Malicious AGENTS.md files have been found in the Downloads folders of some users. If the user is using the Downloads folder as their working directory, an AI agent will read the AGENTS file and download a malicious NPM package.
- 1Password has launched 1Password for Agents, a credential-brokering product that allows agents to access resources for a user without seeing the user’s password,
- Alibaba also donated its OpenSandbox project to AAIF. OpenSandbox is a general-purpose sandbox for running AI models safely.
- The PHP team has released patches for two critical vulnerabilities collectively known as PHP2Shell. However, many sites are running old versions of PHP that need to be upgraded before they can be patched. The maintainers have also released some partial mitigations for sites that can’t upgrade easily, but that won’t fully protect them. Sadly, “the panic hasn’t turned into patching,” and those who don’t patch will pay.
- Brotli isn’t as widely used as PHP, or as old, but a critical flaw in Brotli compression library makes it clear that discovery of hidden vulnerabilities is the shape of things to come. Microsoft has released patches for .Net, PHP maintainers have released patches for PHP, Node.js is also affected, and that’s just the start.
- The private keys of the certificate authority eMudhra have been cracked–not by brilliant cryptography or a quantum computer, but because the keys were generated very poorly. The Chrome and Firefox browsers aren’t trusting the compromised certificates, but almost everything else, including all major package managers, is a problem.
- OpenCode was the victim of a hostile attack in which some users’ API keys and passwords were stolen from their Console service. Its response was hampered by lack of access to AI models without security restrictions.
- The US Department of Homeland Security has banned the use of DeepSeek and applications developed using DeepSeek in all federal agencies.
- To monitor the risks created by the development of frontier models, Anthropic has given six employees of METR access to their models. They continue to work with Accenture and Secure Bio.
- Model abliteration is a poisoning attack in which post-training is used to discover which of a model’s weights corresponds to “no,” and altering them so the model cannot refuse a request. It’s effectively a backdoor into the model’s behavior.
- AWS has launched Strands Box, an open source sandbox that’s designed specifically to prevent AI agents from escaping the sandbox’s control. It includes an open source policy engine, Dogwood, that allows users to place explicit limits on what an agent may do.
- Meta’s Muse, its agent for people who aren’t technology professionals, is a privacy and security disaster.
- Using MCP for communications between agents creates many risks, including new vulnerabilities to prompt injection.
- Google has suspended submissions to the Open Source Software Vulnerability Rewards Program because of the flood of machine-generated vulnerability reports, most of which are (in Google’s words) “not valid.” This suspension should only be temporary.
Infrastructure and operations
There’s been a lot of news about certificate management, not all of it good. It’s time to check on your certificate providers, get ready for quantum-resistant encryption, and automate as much of the process as you can.
- To increase security, the certificate provider Let’s Encrypt will be limiting the lifetime of free certificates to 64 days starting in February 2027. The change should be invisible to sites using automatic certificate management (ACME).
- Crowdflare has announced that it will begin issuing TLS certificates with quantum-resistant encryption. They will continue issuing certificates with classical encryption. Crowdflare hasn’t given a date when they will start issuing the new certificates.
- DeepSeek has open sourced DeepInfer, its inference framework, with an Apache 2.0 license. At present, DeepInfer only supports DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash.
- RemoveMacAI is an open source command-line tool for deleting Apple’s AI from MacOS 27, freeing up 30 GB or so of disk space.
Web
Mark Twain didn’t quite say, “The reports of my death are greatly exaggerated.” But we are hearing that the Web is dead, and that’s indeed an exaggeration. The flood of crawler traffic and the disincentives towards human writing are a problem. But what does “death” mean for a technology so flexible that you can build an office suite that stores entire documents’ URLs?
- TinyLittleOffice.com is a surprisingly complete set of surprisingly capable office applications. It includes a word processor, spreadsheets, and other Office-like apps. Everything is saved in the URL–not on your disk, not in someone’s datacenter. Not suitable for large documents.
- Crowdflare has announced a web search API, now in beta. Although their announcement doesn’t say, we suspect this is an attempt to control web scraping traffic. Matthew Prince, its CEO, has estimated that bot traffic will reach 1000 times human traffic by mid-2027. All of his earlier predictions have been underestimates.
- Jev and its clones have taken the world by storm. Can you beat it at Pacman?
Hardware
- AI labs are heading towards models that can run on phones and similar hardware. Google has compressed Gemma 4 E4B to 5 GB, and Liquid has released LFM2.5-24B-A2B, a 24B mixture-of-experts model with 2B active parameters that also targets devices.
- OpenTPU is an open source API accelerator, designed by AI. Bring your own silicon.
Quantum computing
- Quantinuum has implemented quantum error correction on its latest hardware and has found that it scales well enough to be useful in practice: Adding a physical qubit to a logical cubit cuts the error rate significantly.
- Researchers have discovered a way to read a qubit without collapsing the information it contains into a 1 or 0. Solving this problem (also known as quantum non-demolition or QND) is critical to building quantum computers large enough to do useful work.
Biology
- Watermarking texts is one thing. Google has now designed a watermark for proteins. Like text watermarks, protein watermarks are based on Google’s SynthID.
- Last month we mentioned EEG-capable earbuds. This month, a group of researchers has announced that they have developed an AI application that can reconstruct what someone is seeing from brain scans. The results are impressive, though the privacy implications are chilling.
articles.summary:
The rapid evolution of AI models and agentic tools is reshaping software development and cybersecurity, introducing both advanced capabilities and significant new vulnerabilities for organizations to manage.

### Key Points
- New open-weight models like Kimi 3.1 Pro, Mistral Large 4, and Meta’s Muse series are achieving performance parity with frontier-class AI systems.
- Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google are expanding AI agent standards and interfaces, including the Agent Skills standard and ChatGPT’s Intelligent UI feature.
- Security threats are escalating, highlighted by the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, compromised eMudhra certificate authority keys, and malicious AI agent activity.
- Google has expanded its SynthID watermarking technology to include protein structures, while OpenAI prepares to implement text watermarking to comply with EU regulations.
- The US Department of Homeland Security has banned the use of DeepSeek models across all federal agencies due to emerging security and data privacy concerns.

### Why it Matters
The integration of AI into critical infrastructure and development workflows is creating a complex security landscape where traditional defenses are increasingly insufficient. Organizations must balance the rapid adoption of powerful new models and agents with rigorous security protocols to mitigate risks like prompt injection, data leakage, and supply chain attacks.

articles.title: Binance founder Changpeng Zhao on crypto hack: 'There's no 100% security'
articles.author: Brian Sozzi
articles.content:
It has been a busy few days for Changpeng Zhao in the wake of the hack on the enormous crypto platform he co-founded, Binance.
"It's been a pretty hectic process," Zhao, better known in crypto circles as CZ, told Yahoo Finance. "But the good thing is right now the withdrawals have been restored, the systems back to normal. People are free to use the platform without any issues now. And then all user funds are covered. The users did not suffer any loss."
Binance is the world's largest cryptocurrency trading platform and holds approximately $171 billion in total assets on its platform. The company is led by co-CEOs Richard Teng and Yi Le.
Hackers recently drained roughly $6.3 billion worth of digital assets from Binance on Oct. 29.
Blockchain intelligence firms and the FBI attributed the 20-minute raid with high confidence to TraderTraitor, an elite state-sponsored cyber unit tied to North Korea.
North Korea reportedly denied involvement.
Rather than cracking private cryptographic keys, the attackers reportedly breached internal automated transaction workflows via a Binance employee's laptop.
Read more: How to keep your crypto safe
Binance moved swiftly to stabilize the situation by guaranteeing full customer restitution, deploying corporate treasury reserves, Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) capital, and insurance funds to replenish user balances.
"There's no 100% security," CZ added. "So when you run a platform, especially a crypto platform the possibility is always there. I did not think it was going to be this big of magnitude, probably not."

Binance has restored full platform operations and guaranteed user fund restitution following a major October 29 cyberattack that resulted in the theft of $6.3 billion in digital assets.

### Key Points

- The FBI and blockchain intelligence firms attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, a cyber unit linked to North Korea.
- Attackers bypassed cryptographic keys by compromising an internal employee laptop to access automated transaction workflows.
- Binance utilized corporate treasury reserves, insurance funds, and the Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) to cover all customer losses.
- Binance currently manages roughly $171 billion in total assets and is led by co-CEOs Richard Teng and Yi Le.

This incident highlights the persistent vulnerability of even the world's largest cryptocurrency exchanges to sophisticated, state-sponsored cyber threats. articles.title: What gold's nearly 30% crash from all-time highs tells us about markets and the economy
articles.author: jsor@businessinsider.com (Jennifer Sor)
articles.content:
Gold is barreling toward its worst year in over a decade.
The correction in AI stocks has sucked up investors' attention lately, but it's overshadowed a quiet, dramatic move in gold prices this year. The yellow metal, which was one of the hottest investments in 2025, is down about 29% from its January high, trading below $4,000 an ounce on Tuesday.
The whipsaw is the result of a few things plaguing the US economy and markets this year, from higher rates to a panicked risk-off move in stocks.
Gold is now down 9% for the year — putting it on track for its worst annual performance in 11 years, when it plunged around 10% in 2015. The precious metal also dropped more than 3% in October, marking its worst October since the Great Financial Crisis, according to an analysis from economist David Rosenberg.
It's unusual for gold to sell-off in tandem with stocks. The safe haven is thought to slowly appreciate and provide a safe haven when stocks are volatile or when markets get rocked by geopolitical events. Demand for gold also generally picks up when inflation fears are on the rise, as investors see it as a hedge against a devalued fiat currency, but that hasn't proven true in 2026 either, even as the Iran war causes oil and gas prices to spike.
"Gold is now behaving in too much of a bizarre and unpredictable pattern, and traditional correlations have broken down," Rosenberg wrote this week. "Gold is increasingly behaving like a risk asset, which is an entirely new dynamic."
So, what gives?
There are a few unusual reasons the precious metal has continued to slide this year, even amid circumstances that would normally stoke a rally. Here's what's been driving the decline — and what it says about the US economy and markets, according to analysts.
Yields are higher
While fears of hotter inflation have normally boosted gold prices, higher rate expectations lift Treasury yields and the value of the US dollar, two safe-havens that compete with gold for capital.
Treasury yields are elevated across maturity curve, attesting to ongoing fears about the US fiscal outlook and higher inflation overall. The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield was around 4.91% on Tuesday, up 77 basis points year-to-date.
| US Treasury | Yield | YTD change (in basis points) | 
| 2 year | 4.58% | +111 | 
| 10 year | 4.91% | +77 | 
| 30 year | 5.29% | +43 | 
The weakness in gold also reflects investors' bullishness for the greenback, Rosenberg said, attesting to how markets are focused on the expectation for higher interest rates. The US Dollar Index, which weighs the dollar's value against a basket of other major currencies, ticked up to 101 on Tuesday, up 3% since the start of the year.
What it says about the economy: Higher interest rates are the big story. That's increased the opportunity cost of holding gold, while a stronger US dollar has made it more expensive for international buyers to purchase bullion, Adam Perry, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said.
The Fed put its rate-hiking cycle on pause at its last policy meeting, but investors expect the central bank to resume tightening heading into 2027. Markets are now pricing in a 75% probability the Fed will raise rates another quarter of a percentage point before the end of the year, and a 21% probability that will be followed by another quarter-point hike in January.
Demand for gold is falling
Central banks continue to be major buyers of gold as they diversify their reserves, but demand from other segments is fading. Much of the decline was fueled by people purchasing less physical gold and gold jewelry, the World Gold Council said, noting that bar and coin demand has fallen 19% year-over-year, while global jewelry demand is down 17%.
In the US, gold jewelry revenue is up overall, but unit sales have declined. Gold jewelry growth is concentrated at "higher price points," though "lower-priced merchandise" is underperforming, according to a September report from the analytics firm Tenoris.
What it says about the economy: The K-shaped economy may be playing a role in gold's decline this year, with more aspirational luxury shoppers pulling back on gold purchases as inflation curtails spending. A worldwide slowdown in jewelry and luxury goods may also be a factor, particularly as consumers in the US and China rein in spending overall.
"Whether described as a K-shaped economy, market bifurcation, or a shift in the composition of consumer spending, the data point to a jewelry market increasingly divided by price point," Tenoris wrote in its monthly report.
Gold's decline is largely a rates story, but consumers pulling back certainly "can move the needle," Jose Torres, a senior economist at Interactive Brokers, told Business Insider.
"I think it's been that combination of forces," he said.
The AI sell-off is rippling across markets
Investors may be looking to sell gold to build up more cash on the sidelines, according to Perry. It's a testament to how negative investor sentiment has been lately, given the brutal losses in the AI trade, with the Nasdaq 100 slipping into an official correction and shedding around $2 trillion in market cap since hitting a record in early October.
"This helps explain why gold fell sharply alongside equities on Friday, despite heightened uncertainty," Perry wrote in a note to clients.
Margin calls on tech positions may also have forced investors to sell gold lately, Rosenberg said, noting that those trading on margin may receive calls from their brokerages asking them to deposit more cash to backstop losses on their stock holdings. Debit balances in customers' margin accounts sat near a record high in October, FINRA data shows.
What it says about markets: Risk-off sentiment may be so extreme that investors are selling gold instead of using it as a safe haven.
"Investors liquidating other assets in the process… if you recall, we saw this take hold briefly in the fall of 2008 and after the 9/11 terrorist attacks as well," Rosenberg said.
Investors were also highly exposed to gold after its meme-like rally in 2025, Torres noted.
Gold may be in a yearslong technical holding pattern
Gold has historically seen large upswings before entering a period of near-zero gains, Torres said. He pointed to the metal's double-digit rally in 2025, which mirrored gold's explosive rally coming out of the Great Financial Crisis. The metal stagnated for the following decade before seeing a similar run-up, he noted.
Gold may be entering a similar yearslong technical holding pattern with subdued gains, Torres said, adding that investors may be more focused on other assets, like stocks and real estate, for stronger returns.
"If you just generally don't have the investor demand, then it can't really rally," he said of the outlook for gold.
articles.summary:
Gold prices are on track for their worst annual performance in over a decade, falling 9% this year as investors pivot away from the metal toward higher-yielding assets.

### Key Points
- Gold is trading below $4,000 an ounce, marking a 29% decline from its January peak.
- Rising Treasury yields and a stronger US dollar have increased the opportunity cost of holding gold.
- Global demand for gold bars, coins, and jewelry has dropped significantly, with year-over-year declines of 19% and 17% respectively.
- Investors are liquidating gold holdings to cover margin calls and raise cash following the recent correction in AI-related stocks.
- Markets are pricing in a 75% probability of further Federal Reserve interest rate hikes before the end of the year.

### Why it Matters
The breakdown of gold's traditional role as a safe-haven asset suggests that market sentiment has shifted toward extreme risk-off behavior. This trend indicates that investors are prioritizing liquidity and yield over traditional hedges, potentially signaling a prolonged period of stagnation for the precious metal.

articles.title: iPhone Jailbreak Gets Past Lockdown Mode and Survives an Update
articles.author: Juli Clover
articles.content:
Just over a week after jailbreaking an iPhone Duo on launch day, hacker team Calif is back with another jailbreak demonstration. This time, the group has jailbroken an iPhone in Lockdown Mode, and the jailbreak appears to persist across an iOS update.
Calif shared a video of a jailbroken iPhone 18 Pro with Lockdown Mode on. From there, iOS 27.2 is installed, and the jailbreak remains in place after the update. It isn't clear whether the jailbreak could be installed on a device already running iOS 27.2.
Apple describes Lockdown Mode as "extreme protection" for individuals who might be targeted by sophisticated mercenary spyware. Lockdown Mode disables a long list of features, blocking most message attachment types, limiting web technologies, blocking FaceTime calls from unfamiliar callers, disabling invites for Apple services, and removing location information from photos.
The video shows a malicious PDF sent to the target iPhone using AirDrop to initiate the jailbreak, with the file accepted by the user. Calif hasn't shared additional information, and the exact jailbreak steps are unknown.
Earlier this year, Apple told TechCrunch that it was not aware of any successful mercenary spyware attacks against an iPhone in Lockdown Mode.
Calif previously said it was disclosing vulnerabilities to Apple and did not plan to release a jailbreak tool for end users.
articles.summary:
The hacker team Calif has successfully demonstrated a persistent jailbreak on an iPhone 18 Pro running Apple’s Lockdown Mode, maintaining access even after an iOS 27.2 system update.

### Key Points
- The jailbreak was initiated by sending a malicious PDF file to the target device via AirDrop.
- The exploit remains active on the iPhone 18 Pro following the installation of the iOS 27.2 software update.
- Lockdown Mode is Apple’s security feature designed to protect high-risk users from sophisticated mercenary spyware by restricting system functionality.
- Calif stated it intends to disclose these vulnerabilities to Apple and does not plan to release a public jailbreak tool.
- Apple previously claimed it had no evidence of successful mercenary spyware attacks against devices operating in Lockdown Mode.

### Why it Matters
This demonstration challenges the perceived security of Apple’s Lockdown Mode, which is marketed as an extreme protection measure for high-risk users. If these vulnerabilities are confirmed, it could force Apple to accelerate security patches to maintain user trust in its most restrictive privacy settings.

articles.title: The 4 Elements of Exposure Prioritization and How to Operationalize Them
articles.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
articles.content:
Your team is remediating more vulnerabilities than ever, yet your breach risk has barely changed. You’re spending too much time and effort on exposures attackers may never exploit, while higher-risk exposures sit, waiting in the queue. Gartner®’s report on exposure prioritization states that fewer than 10% of vulnerabilities are exploited, yet most are treated as urgent. The report also argues that CVSS scores alone do not predict actual exploitation or business impact.
Gartner predicts that by 2028, organizations that prioritize exposures using threat intelligence, asset context, exploitability modeling, and security control validation will reduce breach likelihood by at least 70% compared to their peers relying primarily on CVSS-based vulnerability prioritization. Let’s break down how each element works, and how the Picus Platform puts all four into practice.
Severity-based prioritization made sense. Then it didn't.
Severity-driven prioritization was an entirely rational response for the era it was built in: a static attack surface, scarce adversary tooling, and remediation capacity that exceeded disclosure volume. Suddenly, that world is gone. Enterprises face tens of thousands of new vulnerabilities a year across cloud, SaaS, identity, and supply chain modalities, and AI has compressed time-to-exploit from weeks or months to hours.
Gartner is candid about why teams still anchor on severity, and it’s not a lack of awareness. In fact:
- legacy metrics
- compliance pressure, and
- fragmented ownership
all reward what’s auditable over what’s legitimately impactful.
The result is widespread prioritization paralysis, with significant resources being funneled into remediation activity, but with remarkably little measurable risk reduction to show for it.
The smarter path is performing risk-based vulnerability management in its truest sense: measuring success by the exploitable exposures you’ve reduced, not the hypothetical vulnerabilities you’ve closed.
The four elements, and the question each one answers
Gartner’s framework rests on four pillars, and their value emerges only when added together. Sure, operationalizing one or two will bring you incremental gains, but integrating all four delivers significant reductions in both exposure windows and remediation fatigue.
Each element answers a distinct question about an exposure:
An exposure deserves urgent remediation only when all four answers converge.
The model aligns directly with the prioritization and validation stages of continuous threat exposure management (CTEM): remediation is mobilized only after priorities are validated in context.
Element 1: Threat Intelligence
Threat intelligence brings the adversary’s perspective into prioritization by showing which exposures attackers are actually exploiting. In real-world environments, many high-severity vulnerabilities are never exploited. Attackers frequently weaponize moderately rated vulnerabilities because they are easier to exploit, affect widely used systems, or can be exploited reliably. Past exploitation evidence helps teams focus their remediation efforts on a smaller, higher-risk subset of the backlog.
The operational challenge here is speed. Your team needs to use that intelligence to decide what to test and fix before a campaign reaches your environment. Track the time it takes to go from threat publication to testing and remediation.
Element 2: Asset Context and Business Criticality
An exploitable vulnerability becomes materially risky when it affects an asset that supports critical business functions, processes regulated data, or provides an easy pivot to higher-value systems. Without asset context, prioritization treats all assets as equal, and attention can easily drift to low-impact systems while crown-jewel exposures wait in the same queue.
This context already lives in tools most teams own: scanners, CMDBs, cloud security platforms, and identity systems. The practical work is to both unify it and keep it current, so its impact reflects the asset as it’s defended today, not as it appears in an inventory.
Element 3: Exploitability Modeling
Exploit prediction models such as EPSS estimate how likely a vulnerability is to be exploited, based on patterns like exploit complexity, component prevalence, and disclosure-to-exploitation timelines. These models complement threat intelligence by surfacing latent and lingering risks: helping identify the exposures that are statistically likely to be exploited before exploitation is widely observed, enabling you to shift teams from a reactive to an anticipatory or even proactive stance.
Statistical likelihood describes the world in general, not your organization’s unique environment. EPSS points to what’s probably exploitable somewhere; only validation proves what is exploitable here and now. Exploitability modeling works best as a filter that feeds validation, not as a final verdict.
Gartner’s full report goes deeper into how EPSS, KEV and similar models should be weighted against threat intelligence and control validation. Download the Gartner report on exposure prioritization to read the complete analysis.
Element 4: Security Control Validation
This is the element most programs are missing. Security control validation evaluates each exposure against the defenses already deployed around it: segmentation, endpoint protection, detection coverage, and identity controls.
An exposure that looks critical may be practically unreachable behind your existing defenses, while a less critical one on a poorly monitored asset may carry far more risk than its score suggests. Ignoring control context, Gartner warns, leads to systematic overestimation of risk and the wasted remediation efforts that follow it.
Testing shows whether attackers can realistically exploit an exposure in your specific environment today. Gartner notes this capability can be achieved with adversarial exposure validation techniques: proving exploitability with evidence, through live attack execution where testing is safe, and attack-chain analysis against deployed controls where assets can’t be touched.
How Picus Operationalizes All Four Elements into a Single Loop
The sum here is indeed greater than its parts, but the four elements only deliver their full value when evaluated together. This is, not surprisingly, where most organizations struggle as vulnerability management grows into exposure management. Why? Because in most organizations, threat intelligence sits with one team, asset context with another, exploitability scores are in a scanner, and control effectiveness only shows up in periodic assessments. Four inputs in four places do not lead to one decision.
Picus is named among the vendors in the 2026 Gartner® Market Guide for Adversarial Exposure Validation. The Picus Platform brings all four elements together in a continuous loop: Discover, Validate, Prioritize, and Mobilize.
Here’s how the platform maps to each element.
Security control validation deserves a closer look, because evidence is what turns the other three elements from assumptions into decisions. Picus Breach and Attack Simulation is one of three validation methods on the platform.
- Picus Autonomous Penetration Testing runs real exploit paths against reachable production assets and proves which ones lead to your critical systems.
- Picus Exposure Validation breaks each CVE into the techniques an attacker must use and tests every step against your existing controls on that asset, with no exploit fired, so even assets you can never test live get an evidence-backed verdict.
Together, these three validation methods give every exposure one explainable, organization-specific rating.
What Good Looks Like: Measuring the Shift
If prioritization is working, you should be able to see it in three places: your controls hold up better, you respond faster, and your team spends its time on the exposures that matter, rather than wasting it on the ones that don’t.
Here’s what our customers are reporting.
- Within three months of deploying Picus, their security controls are blocking or detecting roughly twice as many attacks as before.
- Response time to emerging threats drops by 89%.
- Missed remediation deadlines on high and critical vulnerabilities fall by 92%, because the queue now holds only the exposures proven to be exploitable.
One customer cut their critical ticket backlog by 98%. And the full cycle, from a new threat or change being detected to actual validated findings landing with the right team, runs under six hours.
A CISO at our 2026 Validation Summit put it simply: While a severity score is a useful label for sorting, the smarter strategy is to shut down those attack paths that could actually hurt your business. The numbers above back this up.
Exposure Prioritization Is a Risk Decision. Make It With Evidence.
Gartner frames exposure prioritization as a risk decision, and we agree.
Each of the four elements answers one part of it: threat intelligence tells you whether the exposure matters to an attacker, asset context tells you what it would cost you, exploitability modeling tells you how likely it is to take place, and security control validation tells you whether it could actually happen here.
The Picus Platform runs all four in one continuous loop, so every exposure ends in a decision you can defend to your board and your auditors: so you can fix it, mitigate it, or accept it with proof.

articles.title: "Steam's review queue is clogged up by AI slop": Salacious Fire Emblem-ish Food Devils gets a delay because its devs think Valve is inundated with genAI games
articles.author: Oisin Kuhnke
articles.content:
You might have seen that for today's grub, Edwin decided to in part feed The Maw with Food Devils, an incredibly salacious, foodie take on Fire Emblem, as it was meant to release today. The only problem is, it's not actually out yet. That might prompt you to call Edwin a rotten liar and march up to his castle at the top of the hill on a dark and stormy night with pitchforks and torches, but I beseech you to wait, because it's actually Steam's fault. And potentially, it's the fault of all those awful AI games that have been flooding Steam recently.
In a Steam blog post shared earlier today, developer Studio Daimon explained why the game isn't able to be released today, first offering a bit of context: if you want to put your game on Steam, you have to submit for approval so that it matches what you've described and doesn't harbour malware, amongst other reasons. As the post explains, "before submitting a build, devs see a disclaimer that says 'This review typically takes 3-5 business days, but please allow up to 7 business days in case feedback needs to be addressed'." Except the team submitted their build on October 12th, more than 20 days ago, with no approval in sight.
The reason? "We can only assume it's because Steam's review queue is clogged up by AI slop, but the whole process is now taking several weeks for some developers." For some context, Game Discovery Tool did some statistics magic and found that more than 50% of games released in October on Steam featured an AI disclosure. Valve have required that games disclose AI use since January 2024, and a year on from then in January 2025 only just over 14% of games featured such a disclosure. In January 2026, that jumped up to a little over 25%, and now here we are at more than 50%.
And to be clear, Steam releases have gone up too. According to SteamDB data, a little over 2000 games were released on the platform in October 2025. But in October 2026, that has jumped up to almost 4000. Correlation is obviously not causation, so take that with a pinch of salt. Still, it paints a concerning image over AI usage, and potentially sounds like it's affecting how Valve operates. Almost as if allowing free reign over AI is bad, or something!
Unfortunately for Studio Daimon, there's no estimate on when Food Devils might launch. "Even now, we don't know when Steam will give us the final OK to finally release our game," they wrote. "We sent another ticket last week saying that the situation was urgent and that we might miss our release date because of this, but it also got ignored. I'm sure that their staff is just too overwhelmed at the moment, but these sudden and massive delays have affected many developers throughout October, with some even being forced to postpone their releases... including us."
They're hoping to still be able to release it by the end of the week, but "can't make any plans or promises because it's out of our control." Perhaps in the meantime, for those who like what's cooking in the devs' kitchen, we could throw the game a wishlist to be ready for whenever it does launch.
articles.summary:
Developer Studio Daimon has delayed the release of its tactical game Food Devils due to significant approval backlogs within the Steam platform's mandatory review process.

### Key Points
- Studio Daimon submitted its game build on October 12, exceeding the standard 3-to-7-day review window by over two weeks.
- The developer attributes the delay to a surge in low-quality AI-generated games flooding the Steam review queue.
- Data shows that over 50% of games released on Steam in October 2026 included AI disclosures, up from 25% in January 2026.
- Monthly game releases on Steam nearly doubled from approximately 2,000 in October 2025 to nearly 4,000 in October 2026.
- Valve has not provided a revised release date for Food Devils, leaving the developer unable to confirm a new launch window.

### Why it Matters
The massive influx of AI-generated content is creating operational bottlenecks that threaten the release schedules of independent developers. This trend highlights growing concerns regarding platform moderation and the sustainability of Steam's current review infrastructure as submission volumes continue to climb.

articles.title: Proton VPN 8.0 is coming to iPhone — and it could be the app's biggest upgrade in years
articles.author: monicajwrites@gmail.com (Monica J. White) , Monica J. White
articles.content:
- Proton VPN has published iOS 8.0.0 on GitHub, but the update is yet to reach the App Store
- Its primary focus is Proton protocols, a new Rust-based VPN engine aimed at stability and censorship resistance.
- An advanced kill switch, an interactive globe map, and better CarPlay support are also on the way.
Proton VPN users on iPhone have a big update to look forward to. The provider has published iOS 8.0.0 on its GitHub releases page, and it could be the most significant change to the app in years.
The biggest addition is Proton protocols, a new VPN architecture that Proton says is designed for improved stability and censorship resistance. It also makes the advanced kill switch possible on iPhone and iPad, a feature that has so far only been available on iOS in beta.
Proton VPN already sits among the best VPN services we've tested, climbing to third place in our latest round of re-testing. Anything that tightens up its iOS app is good news for privacy-minded iPhone owners.
What's new in Proton VPN 8.0 for iOS
The biggest change is one you won't see. Proton protocols, known internally as ProTUN, swaps out the standard wireguard-go code for libpvpnclient, Proton's own WireGuard implementation written in Rust.
Proton says wireguard-go never integrated well with Swift, the language it uses to build its iOS app, which made development and debugging harder.
For users, Proton promises faster updates, fewer platform-specific bugs, and a quicker response when censors change tactics.
The new core also lays the groundwork for post-quantum encryption, which Proton lists as a planned feature. Antonio Cesarano, Product Lead at Proton VPN, says it lets the team experiment with "connection stability, battery usage, and resilience".
A stricter kill switch for your iPhone
A standard kill switch cuts your internet if the VPN connection drops. Proton's advanced kill switch goes further, blocking all internet access unless you're connected to Proton VPN, and it stays active even after you restart your device.
That's a notable step on iOS, where Apple's network restrictions have long made a true kill switch difficult. Proton itself once said a kill switch as it defined it wasn't possible on iOS. Even now, Proton warns that some DNS requests from Apple services can bypass the VPN with the kill switch on.
Version 8.0 also fixes a common frustration. You'll be able to reach LAN devices, like printers, and use Apple CarPlay with either kill switch enabled.
When can you get Proton VPN 8.0?
Proton hasn't announced a release date. However, with the final 8.0.0 build now tagged on GitHub, the App Store rollout could land any time now, though Apple's review process can add a delay.

GPUs are her main area of interest, and nothing thrills her quite like that time every couple of years when new graphics cards hit the market.
She built her first PC nearly 20 years ago, and dozens of builds later, she’s always planning out her next build (or helping her friends with theirs). During her career, Monica has written for many tech-centric outlets, including Digital Trends, SlashGear, WePC, and Tom’s Hardware.

articles.title: We have the most powerful technology in history, and we’re using it to stop hiring young people
articles.author: Mark Minevich
articles.content:
We hold the most powerful technology in human history, and so far corporate America is mostly using it to write marketing copy and cut headcount.
Through September, U.S. employers announced 573,195 job cuts. Artificial intelligence was cited in 120,136 of them, more than any other reason this year, according to outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas. Tech companies alone announced 165,925 cuts, up 54% from the same period last year.
To be fair, total announced cuts are down 39% from the first nine months of 2025, and AI was cited in only about 9% of September’s cuts. The bigger effect is on hiring. Using ADP payroll data, Stanford economists Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar and Ruyu Chen found that as of June, employment among 22- to 25-year-olds in the most AI-exposed occupations was about 19% below where it would be if it had kept pace with young workers in less-exposed jobs. A year earlier, the gap was 15%. They write that the adjustment works “primarily through reduced hiring of young workers rather than increased separations.”
Companies aren’t firing junior workers; they are simply not hiring them. They’re using efficiency as the excuse.
A great economy for whom?
On paper, the economy looks powerful. Real GDP grew at a 3.4% annual rate in the third quarter, up from 2.2% in the second, according to the Bureau of Economic Analysis. Spending on computer equipment, a soft landing for capital expenditure, was a main driver.
But for the common citizen, this year has been anything but a soft landing. Consumer prices rose 3.7% in the year through September, and gasoline rose about 34%. Since the Iran war closed the Strait of Hormuz in March, oil has gone through what the World Bank calls “the largest oil market shock in history.”
In addition, workers now pay an average of $7,471 a year toward family health coverage, up 9% from 2025, according to KFF. Over roughly the same period, wages increased only 3.7%. Effectively, the people took a pay cut.
The looming electricity and water crises
The AI buildout is also competing with households for the same electricity. In PJM, the largest U.S. grid operator, the independent market monitor estimated that data centers caused 63% of the price increase in 2025/2026, about $9.3 billion in costs, according to the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis. Pepco residential customers in Washington, D.C., saw bills rise about $21 a month starting in June 2025. Roughly $10 of that came from capacity prices.
This is what makes me angry. None of these issues requires new technology to be solved. The models exist, the compute exists, and the capital is already being spent. What’s missing is a decision about where to point it.
The American Society of Civil Engineers estimates a water main breaks every two minutes in the U.S., and about 6 billion gallons of treated water is lost daily. We could use AI to forecast load and balance the grid so data centers pay for the strain they add. We could use AI to find leaks in water systems. We could model drought before it reaches a farm, inspect bridges, harden supply chains, and cut diagnosis costs instead of raising premiums.
In June, in the U.K., Northumbrian Water reported that a six-month trial using AI-powered acoustic sensors to help crews locate hidden leaks was saving nearly 6.4 million liters of water a day. This is the technology we must invest in and deploy immediately.
San Jose Water installed 13,600 fixed acoustic sensors across its 2,400-mile network, and the system found 483 leaks and saved more than 400 million gallons of treated water. Plus, New Mexico’s LeakTracer satellite-plus-AI program identified 216 leaks across 181 miles of pipe in its first year. Completing the needed repairs could recover 328 million gallons and save about $505,000 a year.
This must become the industry standard.
Four steps to secure the future
First, we must treat energy resilience as a national security issue. Data centers must be required via litigation to pay for the grid upgrades and capacity they drive. Families shouldn’t have to subsidize the infrastructure required by multibillion-dollar tech companies. AEP Ohio already requires new data-center customers to reimburse 100% of buildout costs if they cancel before energization. The company creating the demand, carrying the risk, must be fundamental.
In my home state, New Jersey’s Data Center Fair Share Act was signed in July 2026, creating a separate rate class for large data centers. This requires them to cover their own infrastructure costs, demands financial guarantees covering at least 85% of requested load for 10 years, and lets them offset capacity obligations by paying for demand reductions elsewhere. This could save ratepayers more than $1 billion a year. Other states are moving in the same direction, with large-load tariffs imposing high minimum-demand charges and contribution-in-aid rules so residential customers aren’t charged if a project underdelivers or exits.
Next, go after health costs at the source. Use AI to reduce the volume of unnecessary tests, procedures, and late-stage interventions rather than simply shifting higher premiums onto households. Start by capping excessive hospital prices in public employee health plans, with safeguards for vulnerable hospitals. Oregon capped in-network hospital payments at twice Medicare’s rates and saved an estimated $107.5 million over 27 months. Then require publicly funded health care AI projects to demonstrate lower costs without compromising care. Efficiency isn’t helping if the patient’s bill remains the same.
Third, deploy AI to retrain people faster than it replaces them. By tying public incentives for AI investment and data-center build-out to measurable entry-level hiring and apprenticeship commitments, AI will create efficiency and jobs. As entry-level roles disappear for the benefit of only AI owners, the coming generations are being steered toward economic ruin. Tie public AI incentives to net-new paid apprenticeships and entry-level jobs, with payments after six and 12 months of verified employment and not simply after a training course.
This isn’t some pipe dream; the blueprint exists. In July, the Labor Department awarded nearly $162 million through an apprenticeship program that links payments to verified retention and progression milestones. Reward employers for being job creators and builders. Going forward, any firm receiving tax credits, accelerated permitting, or public power-purchase support for AI capacity must fund or host a proportional number of paid apprenticeships or entry-level roles, with progress reported publicly.
Finally, give public infrastructure the same AI investment private data centers get. One of the most impactful improvements AI could make is in utilities and water. As governments embed AI into power grids and water systems to stabilize national infrastructure, we should use AI-driven material evaluation of roads and highways and continuous monitoring to predict repair needs before learning from injuries and accidents. Funding can be mandated by dedicating a share of data-center tax revenue to local infrastructure technology. Virginia began taxing data-center electricity consumption at 1.1 cents per kilowatt-hour in July. States should direct a portion of that revenue toward leak detection, grid management, and bridge inspection, plus paying the employees who act on the findings.
A dedicated public AI infrastructure fund can be created and financed by a small, transparent tax on large data-center power or compute capacity, matched by federal and philanthropic capital.
When voters go to the polls Tuesday, they won’t vote on GDP. They’ll vote on whether things at home got easier or harder since their last ballot was dropped in the box. With AI, the question isn’t whether we can point this technology at the problems that decide whether people can afford to live and create a solution. We can do that. The real question is whether anyone in charge is willing to, or if they just want to keep eliminating the future of work for the next generations.
