articles.summary:
U.S. employers are increasingly using artificial intelligence to reduce hiring and cut costs, prompting calls for policy reforms to protect infrastructure, healthcare affordability, and entry-level job opportunities.

### Key Points
- Challenger, Gray & Christmas reported that AI was cited in 120,136 of the 573,195 U.S. job cuts announced through September.
- Stanford economists found that hiring for 22- to 25-year-olds in AI-exposed occupations is 19% lower than in less-exposed sectors.
- Data centers are driving significant electricity price hikes, with the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis estimating they caused $9.3 billion in grid costs.
- Successful AI deployments in water management, such as San Jose Water’s sensor network, have saved hundreds of millions of gallons of treated water.
- New Jersey’s Data Center Fair Share Act and Oregon’s hospital price caps serve as legislative models for mitigating the economic impact of AI and rising costs.

### Why it Matters
The current deployment of AI is prioritizing corporate efficiency and headcount reduction over public infrastructure stability and workforce development. Without policy intervention, the concentration of resources in data centers and the displacement of junior workers threaten long-term economic mobility and the affordability of essential utilities for households.

articles.title: Very cold war: Who’s attacking Europe’s supermarket freezers?
articles.author: Edna Mohamed
articles.content:
Supermarket refrigerators and freezers across Europe have been targeted by a cyberattack that raised the temperature of internet-linked units, destroying and damaging large quantities of food.
On Monday, fridges and freezers at more than 100 shops in several European countries ran hot. Cyberattacks on supermarkets began last month, when hundreds of French supermarkets were left with spoiled food and damage to units which had overheated, costing millions of euros.
So far, it remains unclear why hackers targeted the supermarkets, but attacks have spread across the continent and even to the United States.
Here’s what we know:
Which countries in Europe have been targeted?
On Monday, several supermarkets in Europe were affected, including the following:
- Dutch supermarket operator Delhaize said dozens of its shops in Belgium and Luxembourg were hit by an “IT incident”.
- French retailer Carrefour said about 15 of its 700 Belgian locations were hit by refrigeration problems.
- The Colruyt group, which runs Spar stores in Belgium as franchises, said five of its shops were affected.
- Swedish Coop said cooling systems at seven of its 800 stores were affected, with disruptions ranging from complete shutdowns to partial operation.
- Swedish furniture retailer IKEA, which also operates restaurants at its stores, said one site in Mons, Belgium, had been affected by a cyberattack.
- De Laet & Van Haver, the Belgian butchery chain, said the temperature in its fridges at its store in Hove, south of Antwerp, was raised as high as 18 degrees Celsius, ruining meat worth about 15,000 euros ($16,764).
- The food wholesaler Musgrave said a cyber-incident affected refrigeration systems in 13 of its SuperValu stores in Ireland.
- In October, hundreds of French supermarkets suffered cyberattacks, spoiling tonnes of food, causing fires and melting parts of refrigeration units.
What has happened in the US?
In August, freezers at a market in Fort Huachuca, an Army base in Arizona, went into defrost mode, spoiling all the frozen food they contained, according to a post on Facebook by the base.
The same month, the naval station in Newport, Rhode Island, reported on Facebook that its refrigeration system was affected, leaving only dry goods were available for purchase.
The Pentagon considered the freezer malfunctions on the military bases to be a suspected hack, the Reuters news agency reported late last month, citing four officials close to the matter.
One official said Pentagon investigators were communicating with the French authorities about the issue.
How are cyberattackers targeting fridges and freezers?
Hackers can access the controls of fridges and freezers which use internet software and raise their temperature in order to spoil frozen food.
In some cases, hackers have increased the temperature of appliances to as high as 50C (122F) in European supermarkets, causing them to melt or even catch fire.
Awais Rashid, a professor of cybersecurity at the University of Bristol in the UK, explained that many supermarket refrigeration systems which are remotely managed and, often by third parties, have not been given necessary software updates to prevent hackers.
“In line with established cyber security practices, these systems should be managed via secure networks. However, this is not the case in these incidents and they are accessible on the Internet,” Rashid told Al Jazeera.
“A remote managing party can access a web server on the controller to configure the system including temperature changes and maintenance. There are known vulnerabilities in several controllers (many of which are past their end of life),” he said.
Rashid added that vulnerabilities include “easily guessable” passwords, which would mean anyone could gain access.
Why are hackers doing this?
The motive behind the attacks is unclear, but authorities believe it may be a deliberate attempt to disrupt food supplies.
On Monday, the European Commissioner for Agriculture and Food, Christophe Hansen, said the attacks on fridges were a “deliberate attempt to disrupt” the bloc’s food supply and to undermine consumer confidence.
He added that while “food security is not currently at risk … the food waste and impact on businesses are real”.
Rashid said that while there are few details about who may be behind the attacks or what their motives are, it is likely that these are “the motive here is likely disruption”.
“This has financial impacts on the supermarkets but also societal impacts in terms of security of the food supply chain. Critically, this risks undermining trust in infrastructures on which people rely daily,” he said.
Who is behind the attacks?
On Monday, Belgium’s prosecutor’s office announced that it had opened a criminal investigation into the latest fridge cyberattacks. But so far, no one has taken responsibility.
Theories have emerged linking state actors to cyberattacks generally, with North Korea most recently accused of being behind last week’s $6.3bn Binance cryptocurrency heist, which forced the crypto group to freeze accounts.
European intelligence officials have also warned that Russia is escalating its shadow war on the continent amid the ongoing conflict with Ukraine, with cyberattacks among the methods it uses.
On Tuesday, the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre warned that Britain needs to be prepared for an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered cyberattack on its critical national infrastructure within the next two years.
“By 2028, it is highly likely that Russia, China and other nation states will routinely use AI-cyber to achieve their geopolitical goals, with the UK facing an increase in scale and speed of sophisticated cyberattacks,” the NCSC said in a report.
The report comes shortly after the UK launched its “Be Ready” campaign, calling on citizens to stockpile enough tinned food, bottled water and cash to last three days in the event of a cyberattack or national emergency.
Rashid said that as our infrastructure becomes increasingly digitised, the risk of disruption from cyberattacks, especially “cyber-physical infrastructures such as refrigeration systems”, has risen.
“However, we should also note that a lot of our digital infrastructures operate safely everyday because good security practices enable that. The world works because cyber security works effectively. So it is important that all businesses follow good cyber security practices,” he said.
articles.summary:
Cyberattacks targeting internet-connected refrigeration systems across Europe and the United States have caused widespread food spoilage and equipment damage, prompting investigations into potential efforts to disrupt food supplies.

### Key Points
- Hackers are remotely accessing vulnerable refrigeration controllers to raise temperatures, causing food loss and, in some cases, fires in supermarket units.
- Major retailers including Delhaize, Carrefour, Spar, Coop, IKEA, and SuperValu have reported incidents across Belgium, Luxembourg, France, Sweden, and Ireland.
- U.S. military facilities, including bases in Arizona and Rhode Island, reported similar freezer malfunctions that the Pentagon suspects were deliberate cyberattacks.
- Cybersecurity experts attribute the vulnerabilities to outdated software, lack of secure network management, and the use of easily guessable passwords on remote-access controllers.
- Belgian authorities have launched a criminal investigation into the attacks, though no group has claimed responsibility for the disruptions.

### Why it Matters
These attacks highlight the growing vulnerability of critical infrastructure as essential systems like food refrigeration are increasingly digitized without adequate security protocols. The incidents threaten the stability of the food supply chain and demonstrate how cyber-physical attacks can cause significant financial losses and undermine public trust in essential services.

articles.title: Bitcoin price defends $76K lows as analysts see stocks pricing in ‘political gridlock’
articles.author: Cointelegraph by William Suberg
articles.content:
Bitcoin price defends $76K lows as analysts see stocks pricing in ‘political gridlock’
Bitcoin made modest gains at the start of Wall Street trading on Tuesday as markets awaited cues from the US midterm elections.
Bitcoin (BTC) headed higher at Tuesday’s Wall Street open as a tech-stock rebound under the shadow of uncertainty surrounding the US midterm elections.
Key points:
- Bitcoin price action edged 0.7% higher on Tuesday as US equities avoided succumbing to midterm election uncertainty.
- Analysis from The Kobeissi Letter suggested markets were pricing in two years of political uncertainty amid expectations of Democratic gains in the midterm elections.
- WTI crude oil dipped to $93.59 per barrel, its lowest level since Oct. 15, despite fresh US strikes targeting Iran’s Qeshm Island.
BTC price volatility cools as stocks rise
Data from TradingView showed BTC/USD circling $77,000, continuing to retain local lows near $76,300 seen on Friday.
BTC/USD one-hour chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView
Stocks faced conflicting forces at the start of the US trading session. Apple shares sought to pare losses after falling 4% in premarket trading as the company forecast gross margins of 45% to 46% for the December quarter, down from 47.9% in the previous quarter, citing rising memory-chip costs.
Markets also weighed the potential impact of the US midterm elections on the balance of power in Congress. Although polls suggested significant Democratic gains, some analysts cautioned that the results could be less decisive than expected.
Apple stock one-day chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView
“Investors seem to have a significant dose of skepticism about whether the final outcome is going to be quite as favorable to Democrats as the polling suggests,” Tobin Marcus, head of US policy and politics at equity research company Wolfe Research, told CNBC. Wolfe added that polls were “likely overstating Democratic strength.”
The S&P 500 and tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index finished Monday down 0.5% and 1.1%, respectively. Analysts at trading resource The Kobeissi Letter argued that US political uncertainty, rather than concerns over AI spending alone, was driving market weakness.
“The reality is that the market is pricing-in a major shift in the political landscape of the US,” it wrote on X.
The analysis suggested that a divided Congress could lead to frequent legislative impasses, creating conditions in which policy decisions would become less predictable.
“A change in the political landscape always comes with uncertainty; markets hate uncertainty,” it continued.
“Objectively, the market is in the process of pricing-in two years of political gridlock.” 
Nasdaq Composite Index one-day chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView
Related: Bitcoin price threatens $77.7K support loss with recent buyers underwater
Oil digests latest Iran strike after 7% drop
Oil prices meanwhile brushed off a US attack on Iran’s Qeshm Island, a key military control outpost for the Strait of Hormuz oil route.
The move came just days after US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that President Donald Trump was open to resolving the US-Iran war “diplomatically,” comments that triggered a 7% drop in WTI crude oil on Monday.
WTI initially jumped to $98.80 per barrel before dipping below $94 on Tuesday, hitting its lowest level since Oct. 15.
CFDs on WTI crude oil one-day chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView
articles.summary:
Bitcoin prices held steady near $76,000 during Tuesday’s Wall Street opening as investors navigated market volatility and uncertainty surrounding the potential impact of the United States midterm elections.

### Key Points
- Bitcoin traded near $77,000, maintaining support levels established during the previous week's market activity.
- Analysts at The Kobeissi Letter suggest financial markets are currently pricing in two years of potential political gridlock in Washington.
- Apple shares faced downward pressure after the company forecasted lower gross margins for the December quarter due to rising memory-chip costs.
- WTI crude oil prices fell to $93.59 per barrel, marking the lowest valuation since October 15 despite recent US military strikes near Iran.
- The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite Index experienced recent declines as investors weighed conflicting economic data and political polling results.

### Why it Matters
The current market behavior reflects a broader investor strategy to hedge against the unpredictability of a divided US Congress. By pricing in potential legislative impasses, traders are signaling that political instability remains a primary driver of volatility across both cryptocurrency and traditional equity sectors.

articles.title: Microsoft made Windows 11 more responsive on these 8GB laptops
articles.author: c.cale.hunt@gmail.com (Cale Hunt) , Cale Hunt
articles.content:
Microsoft has been busy at work reducing the amount of RAM that Windows 11 consumes, and it finally made an official statement today on the topic.
As it turns out, the company has already been quietly shipping performance improvements in the latest Windows 11 updates, focusing on making systems with 8GB of RAM feel a lot more responsive.
The result? Microsoft says Windows 11 is now about 20% more responsive on 8GB PCs compared to before this work started. The work also applies to systems with 4GB, 16GB, and beyond, with specific tuning for each amount.
This couldn't come at a better time. RAM and storage shortages (explained below) are driving up the cost of all PCs, and models with 8GB of RAM are being revived to lessen the burden on consumers.
Our favorite 8GB Windows laptops in November 2026
Why you can trust Windows Central
Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.
Companies like Dell, Acer, and HP have all recently launched 8GB laptops that cost somewhere around $699, with student and regular discounts frequently dropping those numbers lower.
If you were hesitant to shop for an 8GB laptop before, the recent Windows 11 updates should have you reconsidering, especially when prices are this reasonable. Here are my three favorite 8GB laptops right now.
Dell's awesome XPS 13 starts at $699.99 (or $599.99 if you're a student) and includes an Intel Core 5 320 CPU, 8GB of LPDDR5x RAM, a 256GB M.2 PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD, and a 13.4-inch touch display with 2560x1600 resolution
Dell's new XPS 13 for 2026 wowed both Zac Bowden and me at Computex earlier this year, and it's been available to buy since June.
It's a laptop with many premium features despite its price, including a higher-res 2560x1600 (QHD+) display with a 120Hz refresh rate, an IR camera for Windows Hello facial recognition, capable speakers, and a comfortable keyboard/touchpad combo.
It does not, however, offer USB-A or 3.5mm audio ports. Its display does not use an OLED panel; it uses IPS instead. And the $599 price is only available for students.
Still, $699 for everyone else is not bad at all in this economy, and most users should have no issues with the XPS 13.
HP's 14-inch OmniBook 5 is currently on sale for $599.99. It has an Intel Core 5 320 CPU, 8GB of LPDDR5x RAM, a 256GB M.2 PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD, and a 14-inch OLED touch display with 1920x1200 resolution.
HP's OmniBook 5 14 comes with the same Intel Core 5 320 CPU as the other laptops in this roundup, so don't expect any major performance changes.
The OmniBook 5 includes an OLED panel for deeper contrast and more vivid color than IPS. The tradeoff is a lower 1920x1200 resolution and lower 60Hz refresh rate compared to the XPS 13.
HP's laptop also includes HDMI and 3.5mm audio ports alongside dual USB-C at 10Gbps. It's nice to have native video, but the lack of Thunderbolt is a letdown.
This laptop is currently on sale for $599.99 for everyone, making it (temporarily) the best deal of the bunch.
Acer's Swift Air 14 immediately makes an argument for itself with twice as much storage (512GB) as the Dell and HP laptops. For those who prefer to store locally, this could be the deciding factor. However, it does drop down to PCIe 3.0 speeds.
Performance is largely the same thanks to it having the Intel Core 5 320 chip inside, with 8GB of LPDDR5x RAM.
The display hits a 1920x1200 resolution; it doesn't have touch, but it does hit a smoother 120Hz refresh rate. You're definitely giving up some screen quality to land that extra storage.
While the keyboard is great, the touchpad leaves something to be desired. Your experience may vary.
Why is Microsoft concerned with reducing Windows 11 RAM usage?
Sure, Windows 11 could always be more streamlined, but this big push for more RAM efficiency is also a result of the ongoing memory and storage crisis.
See, AI data centers are eating up many of the foundational components of PCs, making the consumer side far more expensive.
RAM in particular has exploded in price; the same 32GB kit of DDR5 I bought for my gaming PC a few years ago, for example, is roughly 600% more expensive today. Storage isn't much better.
This is forcing PC makers to reevaluate their product lineups, as many consumers can no longer afford PCs with 16GB or more of RAM.
Cutting RAM in half is a huge cost saver and won't likely stop anytime soon (the RAM crisis could last for years to come), so it's great to see Microsoft taking user complaints about Windows 11's responsiveness (or lack thereof) seriously.
Join us on Reddit at r/WindowsCentral to share your insights and discuss our latest news, reviews, and more.
Cale Hunt brings to Windows Central more than nine years of experience writing about PC gaming, Windows laptops, accessories, and beyond. If it runs Windows or in some way complements the hardware, there’s a good chance he knows about it, has written about it, or is already busy testing it.
articles.summary:
Microsoft has optimized Windows 11 to improve system responsiveness by 20% on devices with 8GB of RAM, helping maintain performance amid rising global hardware and memory costs.

### Key Points
- Microsoft updated Windows 11 to enhance efficiency for systems with 4GB, 8GB, and 16GB of RAM.
- The performance improvements aim to mitigate the impact of rising component costs driven by high demand for AI data centers.
- Major manufacturers including Dell, HP, and Acer are currently offering 8GB laptops priced between $599 and $699.
- Specific models highlighted include the Dell XPS 13, HP OmniBook 5, and Acer Swift Air 14, all featuring Intel Core 5 320 processors.

### Why it Matters
These optimizations allow budget-conscious consumers to maintain a smooth computing experience on entry-level hardware despite the ongoing global memory and storage crisis. By reducing the resource footprint of Windows 11, Microsoft is helping PC manufacturers keep affordable 8GB laptops viable in a market where high-end memory prices have surged.

articles.title: Google Drops the Hammer: What the Videostrong Scandal Means for Your Streaming Boxes
articles.author: Andrew Allen
articles.content:
If you have a Mecool smart TV box plugged into your living room setup, a recent bombshell announcement from Google and its Threat Intelligence Group demands your attention. Google recently dismantled a massive, global cybercrime operation, dubbed the “XCPE botnet” that turned over 1.3 million consumer devices into secret spy and ad-fraud gadgets.
At the center of this massive security breach is a hardware manufacturer called Videostrong, and its popular consumer-facing subsidiary, Mecool. For the average consumer, corporate terms like “botnets” and “firmware backdoors” can sound intimidating. However, understanding what went wrong is critical to keeping your home network safe.
What Did Videostrong Do?
According to Google’s detailed technical report, hardware maker Videostrong deliberately embedded a hidden backdoor (the XCPE malware) directly into the core system software of its devices over a period of years.
Instead of a typical hacker breaking into a device after purchase, this threat was built right into the factory code. Videostrong allegedly used this hidden access to monetize the devices behind the owners’ backs. They sold remote access to criminal groups, turning everyday living room boxes into tools for:
- Residential Proxy Networks: Selling your home internet bandwidth to unknown third parties (using modules like Linkfog, AppSalt, NetNut, and GaGaNode) so traffic could be routed through your IP address.
- Ad-Fraud Engines: Quietly running background applications with transparent window overlays and hidden WebViews to simulate human web traffic, clicks, and video views to steal advertising money.
- Deep Surveillance: Granting operators the ability to capture live screenshots, inject keystrokes, execute shell commands, and exfiltrate system logs and sensitive device data.
How Does This Affect the Mecool Subsidiary and Everyday Users?
For everyday shoppers, Mecool is the most widely recognized brand tied to Videostrong. Mecool manufactures popular Android TV set-top boxes frequently bought online for streaming.
Because of these severe infractions, Google has taken swift, definitive action:
- The Death Penalty for the Brand: Google has permanently banned Videostrong—along with any of its subsidiaries, partners, and future affiliates (including Mecool)—from building or selling certified Android devices, or supplying software to other certified vendors.
- Compromised Hardware: Security firms analyzing the fallout note that many popular Mecool-branded boxes were shipped with this backdoor pre-installed.
- The Hard Truth for Owners: Because the malware runs as a system-level application signed with the manufacturer’s own keys, security experts warn that average users cannot remove it. If you clear the system or factory reset the device, the malware automatically reinstalls itself from the core firmware.
What Should You Do Next?
If you own a Mecool streaming box or a generic Android TV box linked to Videostrong, cybersecurity experts recommend treating the device as completely compromised. The safest course of action is to unplug the device, disconnect it from your network, and safely dispose of it. Additionally, it is wise to change your home Wi-Fi password to clear out any lingering digital access.
Google’s decisive shutdown is a major win for internet safety, but it serves as a stark reminder: always buy smart home tech from trusted, mainstream brands with proven track records for supply-chain security.
articles.summary:
Google has permanently banned hardware manufacturer Videostrong and its subsidiary Mecool after discovering a pre-installed backdoor that turned 1.3 million Android TV boxes into a global botnet.

### Key Points
- Google’s Threat Intelligence Group dismantled the XCPE botnet, which utilized hidden firmware backdoors to facilitate ad fraud and residential proxy services.
- The malware allowed unauthorized third parties to capture screenshots, log keystrokes, and execute shell commands on compromised devices.
- Videostrong and its subsidiary, Mecool, are now prohibited from producing or supplying certified Android devices.
- Security experts state the malware is embedded in the core firmware, making it impossible for users to remove via factory resets.
- Owners of affected Mecool streaming boxes are advised to disconnect the devices from their networks and dispose of them immediately.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights significant supply-chain security risks when purchasing smart home hardware from less-regulated manufacturers. Consumers should prioritize established brands to avoid devices that may compromise home network privacy and security through pre-installed malicious software.

articles.title: A Binance engineer thought he was interviewing for a job. Then the hackers pounced
articles.author: Rafael Nam
articles.content:
A Binance engineer thought he was interviewing for a job. Then the hackers pounced
The massive $6.3 billion cyber heist suffered by crypto exchange Binance last week may have taken place in only about twenty minutes — but the attacks were months in the making.
That's according an initial assessment released by Binance on Tuesday about how it suffered the world's biggest-ever cyber heist by hackers the FBI has identified as being a North Korean state-sponsored unit.
Those findings show the hackers first tried testing and penetrating Binance's security systems back in June, though the crypto exchange was able to detect that attempt and stop it.
Though unsuccessful, that attempt allowed the hackers — identified by the FBI as a North Korean military unit called TraderTraitor — to learn more about Binance and its systems.
Then, the hackers tried again. In September, a Binance engineer was contacted in a job-hunting platform by a person posing as a "project director" from a company that turned out to be fictious.
The engineer then conducted a first-round interview with a supposed HR representative from the fake company. The hackers used this interview to "build trust," with the Binance employee, the exchange said. The interviewer even shared supposed social media accounts, as well as personal photos and videos with the Binance engineer.
"This was more advanced and deceptive than previously seen social engineering approaches," Binance said in its assessment.
Then hackers pounced
The engineer was then told he would be conducting a second interview with the supposed CEO of the company in a popular social chat app. It was in this interview that the Binance employee — who was at his work laptop — was asked to download "an assignment" as part of the job recruitment process.
Instead, the "assignment" contained malicious code that allowed hackers to build out an attack that culminated last week when hackers made off with over $6 billion worth of crypto currencies held by Binance's customers at the exchange.
Binance said in the statement posted on X that the company is taking a series of actions, including an independent cybersecurity review to prevent future attacks. On Monday the exchange had said it had already replaced most of the stolen crypto currencies stolen by customers using its own funds.
"This should not have happened," Binance said in its assessment on Tuesday. "And we apologise for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry."
articles.summary:
North Korean state-sponsored hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance after compromising an engineer’s work laptop through a sophisticated social engineering scheme disguised as a legitimate job recruitment process.

### Key Points
- The FBI identified the attackers as TraderTraitor, a North Korean military unit that previously attempted to breach Binance systems in June.
- Hackers gained access by posing as recruiters and tricking a Binance engineer into downloading malicious software during a fake job interview.
- The cyber heist resulted in the loss of $6.3 billion in customer cryptocurrency assets, marking the largest theft in the industry's history.
- Binance has committed to using its own funds to reimburse affected customers and is conducting an independent cybersecurity review to prevent future incidents.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights the increasing sophistication of state-sponsored social engineering attacks targeting high-value employees at major financial institutions. It underscores the critical need for enhanced endpoint security and rigorous verification protocols to protect digital assets from evolving cyber threats.

articles.title: Millions of Android TV boxes came with malware, and Google's certification missed it
articles.author: Hamed Paydarfar
articles.content:
Summary
- XCPE backdoor preinstalled on 1.3M set-top boxes by Videostrong, creating a botnet for fraud, theft and traffic routing
- Videostrong passed Google's certification by hiding malware that activated only after the first boot.
- Google says it has now cut ties with Videostrong and tightened reviews.
Google and its partners recently shared the news of a now-dismantled backdoor that was preinstalled on more than 1.3 million set-top boxes, turning them into nodes in a botnet. According to the company's official report, the XCPE malware was deliberately deployed by Videostrong, which is an Android device manufacturer.
The backdoor was built directly into the firmware of the affected models over several years. Infected boxes were used for things like ad fraud and data theft. Moreover, units had the ability to route other people's traffic through the owner's internet connection, which put anyone using the same network as an infected Android TV box at risk.
These boxes passed Google's certification for years
And it makes you wonder what else is still out there that Google doesn't know about
This is certainly not a first for Google, and we can only hope such a large-scale malicious operation is not to be repeated. A very concerning detail is that Videostrong was allowed to manufacture certified Android devices with Google apps. This means the company passed Google's required security testing that all hardware partners of the company have to go through.
Google says Videostrong used obfuscation to exploit a gap in those tests. The malicious code was designed to load only after the device's first boot — a sophisticated trick from the bad guys, indeed. At the same time, it's only natural to raise eyebrows at the questionable series of security and QC checks that failed to catch the malware for years. Checking what the firmware does after first boot should be a bare-minimum precaution. The whole purpose of a certificate is to assure buyers that someone has inspected what they are plugging into their TVs and using to sign in to their Google accounts.
Unfortunately, this is not an isolated weak point, and Google never fails to give us all a shock with news like this now and then. Very recently, Google promoted a fake Chrome app on its official store that showcased a six-figure download count despite copying the real browser's name, icon, and screenshots. While different, these two cases show how such threats can slip through Google-controlled security gates that users reasonably assume have already covered the basics.
Google now says it has cut ties with Videostrong and banned it from producing certified Android devices. It also says it has changed its review process to ensure nothing like this happens again. Google recommends purchasing set-top boxes only from reputable manufacturers that the company lists as official Android TV partners. While you're at it, Google, how about double-checking that list of certification holders, too?
Ordinary smart-TV privacy settings can reduce tracking without breaking major features, but they can't neutralize malware embedded in the firmware. Ideally, a certification should be more than boastful a logo on the packaging. Yet, Google’s security bolts were evidently not tight enough to catch something buyers had every reason to assume was being checked.
articles.summary:
Google has dismantled a massive botnet involving 1.3 million Android set-top boxes manufactured by Videostrong, which contained preinstalled XCPE malware designed to facilitate ad fraud and data theft.

### Key Points
- The XCPE backdoor was embedded directly into the firmware of devices manufactured by Videostrong.
- Infected set-top boxes were used to conduct ad fraud, steal data, and route unauthorized traffic through users' home networks.
- Videostrong bypassed Google’s security certification by using obfuscation to trigger the malware only after the device's initial boot.
- Google has officially terminated its partnership with Videostrong and banned the company from producing certified Android devices.
- The tech giant has updated its security review processes to better detect malicious code hidden within device firmware.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights significant vulnerabilities in the supply chain for consumer electronics and raises concerns regarding the efficacy of Google’s hardware certification standards. It serves as a reminder that even officially certified devices can pose serious security risks, potentially compromising user privacy and home network integrity.

articles.title: The FBI Says North Korean Hackers Stole $6.3 Billion from Binance, and Kim Jong Un’s Sister Calls It a ‘Grave Political Provocation’
articles.author: January Nelson
articles.content:
The FBI says the group behind Binance’s $6.3 billion cryptocurrency theft is TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking operation also known as the Lazarus Group. Kim Yo Jong, the sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, has rejected the accusation and accused the US of using cybercrime allegations to damage her country’s reputation.
“It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads the international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds,” Kim said. She said opposing malicious activity in cyberspace remains government policy.
The Secret Service and blockchain security researchers have also attributed the attack to North Korea. The FBI has asked cryptocurrency companies to stop transactions tied to accounts associated with the group, which was previously blamed for the $1.5 billion Bybit theft in 2025. That attack held the crypto theft record before the Binance hack.
Binance says its preliminary investigation points to a compromised engineer’s laptop that gave attackers a way to withdraw funds without authorization. The exchange has pledged to cover every loss from the incident and says it’s already replaced about 95% of the stolen assets.
After transactions resumed on November 1, a Binance spokesperson said net withdrawals had reached $4.72 billion. The spokesperson called that a “relatively limited portion” of roughly $157 billion in total assets and said: “Withdrawal levels are stabilising to what we would consider normal and expected on-chain activity.”
North Korea has repeatedly denied responsibility for major cyberattacks. Those denials have come amid allegations that its hacking operations help finance its heavily sanctioned economy. Talented students are recruited by North Korea into hacking units supervised by its intelligence services, research groups say.

articles.summary:
The FBI has officially attributed the $6.3 billion cryptocurrency theft from Binance to the North Korean hacking group TraderTraitor, despite formal denials from the nation’s leadership.

### Key Points
- The FBI and U.S. Secret Service identified the Lazarus Group, also known as TraderTraitor, as the perpetrator behind the Binance breach.
- Binance reported that the theft occurred after an engineer’s laptop was compromised, allowing unauthorized access to platform funds.
- The exchange has pledged to cover all losses and has already replaced approximately 95% of the stolen assets.
- Following the resumption of transactions on November 1, Binance experienced $4.72 billion in net withdrawals.
- North Korean official Kim Yo Jong denied the allegations, claiming the accusations are a political provocation intended to damage the country's reputation.
- This incident surpasses the $1.5 billion Bybit theft in 2025, which previously held the record for the largest cryptocurrency heist.

### Why it Matters
This massive security breach highlights the growing vulnerability of major cryptocurrency exchanges to state-sponsored cyber operations aimed at bypassing international economic sanctions. The incident underscores the significant financial risks facing digital asset platforms and the ongoing challenge of securing global financial infrastructure against sophisticated, government-backed hacking units.

articles.title: 2026 Hackaday Supercon: Bruce Potter’s Keynote Explores the Hacker Mind
articles.author: Tom Nardi
articles.content:
What is hacking? Many, especially in the mainstream, view it through the lens of computer security. Others consider it synonymous with making or creating. Even for those of us immersed in the community, this can be a surprisingly difficult question to answer.
In his Hackaday Supercon 2026 keynote address, Bruce Potter will explore this idea by taking a step back and looking at what makes someone a hacker in the first place. Rather than viewing hacking as a singular act, he’ll make the case that it’s a mindset, a way of approaching problems that’s not strictly dependent on the tools used or even the desired outcome.
With a cybersecurity career that’s spanned three decades, Bruce has been involved with hacking at every level and in every form — from conducting DARPA research to founding The Shmoo Group and helping organize the legendary ShmooCon. Currently the Chief Product Officer at Trinity Cyber, Bruce has made creative problem solving his life’s work, and he’s eager to share what he’s learned with the Hackaday community. While most of us won’t get the opportunity to advise on national cybersecurity policy as he has, we can still apply the same techniques to our own personal and professional projects.
Those joining us this weekend in Pasadena will get to experience Bruce’s keynote, as well as more than 30 other fascinating presentations, with a group of individuals who are just as eager to understand the how and why of the world around them as you are. Making personal connections with like-minded folks is truly the highlight of Hackaday Supercon; badge hacking and tacos are just the fringe benefits.
In our totally unbiased opinion, we believe Hackaday Supercon is the ultimate hardware hacking conference, but you don’t have to take our word for it. A few tickets are still left if you want to see for yourself.
articles.summary:
Cybersecurity expert Bruce Potter will deliver the keynote address at the 2026 Hackaday Supercon in Pasadena, exploring the core mindset and creative problem-solving philosophy behind modern hacking.

### Key Points
- Bruce Potter, Chief Product Officer at Trinity Cyber, will headline the 2026 Hackaday Supercon event.
- The keynote focuses on defining hacking as a versatile mindset rather than a specific set of technical tools.
- Potter’s career includes three decades of experience, ranging from DARPA research to co-founding the ShmooCon security conference.
- The weekend event in Pasadena features over 30 presentations centered on hardware hacking and collaborative engineering.
- Limited tickets remain available for attendees interested in the conference's technical workshops and community networking opportunities.

### Why it Matters
This keynote highlights the evolution of hacking from a narrow security focus to a broader methodology for creative problem-solving in professional and personal projects. By framing hacking as a mindset, the event encourages engineers and hobbyists to apply these analytical techniques to diverse technical challenges.
